questions.q: What is the defining feature of AWS Secrets Manager compared to Parameter Store?
options: Built-in automatic rotation for supported services such as Amazon RDS
It is the only AWS service that can store an API key
It is completely free to use regardless of secret count
It does not require any authentication to retrieve a secret
questions.explain: Secrets Manager can automatically generate a new credential and update both the service (like RDS) and the stored value on a schedule, with no manual step.

questions.q: How does an application avoid breaking when Secrets Manager rotates a database password automatically?
options: It always fetches the current value from Secrets Manager at connection time instead of storing the password itself
It caches the password permanently the first time it connects
It must be manually restarted every time rotation occurs
Rotation only happens if the application explicitly requests it
questions.explain: Because the app asks for the current secret value at connection time, it never notices that the password changed underneath it overnight.

questions.q: What makes Systems Manager Parameter Store's Standard tier appealing for ordinary configuration values?
options: It is free for a generous number of parameters and API calls
It automatically rotates every parameter on a schedule
It can only store values up to one character long
It requires a separate AWS account to use
questions.explain: The Standard tier's generous free usage makes Parameter Store the default choice for feature flags, hostnames, and other non-sensitive configuration.

questions.q: What is a SecureString parameter in Parameter Store?
options: A basic secret value type encrypted with AWS KMS, usable for simple secrets without Secrets Manager's rotation features
A parameter that can only hold numeric values
A feature exclusive to AWS Secrets Manager, not Parameter Store
A parameter type that is never encrypted
questions.explain: SecureString lets Parameter Store hold basic secrets, encrypted with KMS -- but rotating one requires custom scripting since there's no built-in rotation workflow.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why might a team use Secrets Manager for a production RDS password but Parameter Store for an internal hostname?
options: The password needs scheduled rotation (worth Secrets Manager's cost), while the hostname doesn't need rotation and is covered free by Parameter Store
Parameter Store cannot store any secret values at all
Secrets Manager is always the cheaper option for every use case
Hostnames must legally be stored only in Secrets Manager
questions.explain: The choice comes down to which property the value needs -- rotation for the password justifies Secrets Manager's cost, while the hostname doesn't need it and Parameter Store is free.
